To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) GCL with popular contrastive augmentations is bounded in performance by the amount of style present in the data, and (ii) reconstruction-based approaches are more robust to style and perform better in low-style scenarios.
the success of graph contrastive learning is bounded by the edit distance of the data and reconstruction-based methods are expected to be better suited for tasks with low style vs. content ratios.
the success of contrastive methods is bounded by the similarity between different classes, and that reconstruction methods are more robust to style variation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and analyzing graph representation learning methods.
understanding the conditions under which different graph representation learning paradigms succeed and failing.
understanding the conditions that lead to successful self-supervised graph learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance of GCL is bounded by the amount of style information and the performance of reconstruction-based approaches is bounded by the ratio of style vs. node features.

the reconstruction-based approaches perform better than GCL when the style vs content ratio is low, but GCL performs better than the reconstruction-based approaches when style and content are more balanced.
the reconstruction-based methods perform better when the data is less noisy and GCL with augmentation performs better when the data has more noise, but the data is still not too noisy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GCL with popular augmentation methods is better when there is a large amount of style in a dataset, and that reconstruction-based methods are better when there is more content.
we provide a theoretical framework and a synthetic data generation procedure to understand when different self-supervised graph learning approaches work.

the performance of a self-supervised graph learning paradigm is bounded by how much information is shared between different graph instances and that reconstruction approaches are expected to perform well when the amount of shared information is low.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no one-size-fits-all approach to graph representation learning, but that the choice of a method should be guided by the dataset properties and downstream tasks.
there is no universal best paradigm for graph representation learning.
GCL with popular augmentation strategies is a good fit for downstream tasks where there is moderate style and the graph edit distance is small between different classes.
